{{Short description|Digital signature scheme}}
In [[hash-based cryptography]], the '''Merkle signature scheme''' is a [[Digital signature|digital signature scheme]] based on [[Merkle tree]]s (also called hash trees) and one-time signatures such as the [[Lamport signature|Lamport signature scheme]]. It was developed by [[Ralph Merkle]] in the late 1970s<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merkle |first=Ralph |date=1979 |title=Secrecy, authentication and public key systems |url=http://www.ralphmerkle.com/papers/Thesis1979.pdf |journal=Ph.D. Dissertation |pages=32–61}}</ref> and is an alternative to traditional digital signatures such as the [[Digital Signature Algorithm]] or [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]]. [[NIST]] has approved specific variants of the Merkle signature scheme in 2020.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2020/stateful-hash-based-signature-schemes-sp-800-208 | title=Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes: SP 800-208 &#124; CSRC | date=30 October 2020 }}</ref>

An advantage of the Merkle signature scheme is that it is believed to be resistant against attacks by [[quantum computer]]s. The traditional [[Public-key cryptography|public key]] algorithms, such as RSA and [[ElGamal signature scheme|ElGamal]] would become insecure if an effective quantum computer could be built (due to [[Shor's algorithm]]). The Merkle signature scheme, however, only depends on the existence of secure [[hash function]]s. This makes the Merkle signature scheme very adjustable and resistant to quantum computer-based attacks. The Merkle signature is a ''one time signature'' with finite signing potential. The work of [[Moni Naor]] and [[Moti Yung]] on signature based [[one-way permutation]]s and functions (and the invention of [[universal one-way hash function]]s) gives a way to extend a Merkle-like signature to a complete signature scheme.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Naor |first1=Moni |last2=Yung |first2=Moti |date=1989 |title=Universal One-Way Hash Functions and their Cryptographic Applications |url=https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/uowhf.pdf |journal=[[Symposium on Theory of Computing]] |pages=33–43}}</ref>

==Key generation==
The Merkle signature scheme can be used to sign a limited number of messages with one public key <math>\text{pub}</math>. The number of possible messages must be a power of two, so we denote the possible number of messages as <math>N = 2^n</math>.

The first step of generating the public key <math>\text{pub}</math> is to generate <math>N</math> private/public key pairs <math>(X_i, Y_i)</math> of some one-time signature scheme (such as the Lamport signature scheme). For each <math>1 \leq i \leq 2^n</math>, a hash value of the public key <math>h_i = H(Y_i)</math> is computed.

[[Image:MerkleTree1.1.svg|thumb|300px|Merkle Tree with 8 leaves]]

With these hash values <math>h_i</math> a [[Merkle tree|hash tree]] is built, by placing these <math>2^n</math> hash values as leaves and recursively hashing to form a binary tree. Let <math>a_{i,j}</math> denote the node in the tree with height <math>i</math> and left-right position <math>j</math>. Then, the hash values <math>h_i = a_{0,i}</math> are the leaves. The value for each inner node of the tree is the hash of the concatenation of its two children. For example, <math>a_{1,0} = H(a_{0,0} || a_{0,1})</math> and <math>a_{2,0} = H(a_{1,0} || a_{1,1})</math>.  In this way, a tree with <math>2^n</math> leaves and <math>2^{n+1} - 1</math> nodes is built.

The private key of the Merkle signature scheme is the entire set of <math>(X_i, Y_i)</math> pairs. A shortcoming with the scheme is that the size of the private key scales linearly with the number of messages to be sent.

The public key <math>\text{pub}</math> is the root of the tree, <math>a_{n,0}</math>.  The individual public keys <math>Y_i</math> can be made public without breaking security. However, they are not needed in the public key, so they can be kept secret to minimize the size of the public key.

==Signature generation==
To sign a message <math>M</math> with the Merkle signature scheme, the signer picks a key pair <math>(X_i, Y_i)</math>, signs the message using the one-time signature scheme, and then adds additional information to prove that the key pair used was one of the original key pairs (rather than one newly generated by a forger).

[[Image:MerkleTree2.1.svg|thumb|300px|Merkle tree with path A and authentication path for i&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, n&nbsp;=&nbsp;3]]

First, the signer chooses a <math>(X_i, Y_i)</math> pair which had not previously been used to sign any other message, and uses the one-time signature scheme to sign the message, resulting in a signature <math>\text{sig}'</math> and corresponding public key <math>Y_i</math>. To prove to the message verifier that <math>(X_i, Y_i)</math> was in fact one of the original key pairs, the signer simply includes intermediate nodes of the Merkle tree so that the verifier can verify <math>h_i = a_{0,i}</math> was used to compute the public key <math>a_{n,0}</math> at the root of the tree.  The path in the hash tree from <math>a_{0,i}</math> to the root is <math>n + 1</math> nodes long. Call the nodes <math>A_0, \ldots, A_n</math>, with <math>A_0 = a_{0,i} = H(Y_i)</math> being a leaf and <math>A_n = a_{n,0} = \text{pub}</math> being the root.

<math>A_i</math> is a child of <math>A_{i+1}</math>. To let the verifier calculate the next node <math>A_{i+1}</math> given the previous, it needs to know the other child of <math>A_{i+1}</math>, the sibling node of <math>A_i</math>. We call this node <math>\text{auth}_i</math>, so that <math>A_{i+1} = H(A_i || \text{auth}_i)</math>. Hence, <math>n</math> nodes <math>\text{auth}_0, \ldots, \text{auth}_{n-1}</math> are needed, to reconstruct <math>A_n = a_{n,0} = \text{pub}</math> from <math>A_0 = a_{0,i}</math>.  An example of an authentication path is illustrated in the figure on the right.

Together, the nodes <math>\text{auth}_{0}, \ldots, \text{auth}_{n-1}</math>, the <math>Y_i</math>, and the one-time signature <math>\text{sig}'</math> constitute a signature of <math>M</math> using the Merkle signature scheme: <math>\text{sig} = (\text{sig}' || Y_i || \text{auth}_0 || \text{auth}_1 || \ldots || \text{auth}_{n-1})</math>.

Note that when using the Lamport signature scheme as the one-time signature scheme, <math>\text{sig}'</math> contains a part of the private key <math>X_i</math>.

==Signature verification==
The verifier knows the public key <math>\text{pub}</math>, the message <math>M</math>, and the signature <math>\text{sig} = (\text{sig}' || Y_i || \text{auth}_0 || \text{auth}_1 || \ldots || \text{auth}_{n-1})</math>. First, the verifier verifies the one-time signature <math>\text{sig}'</math> of the message <math>M</math> using the one-time signature public key <math>Y_i</math>. If <math>\text{sig}'</math> is a valid signature of <math>M</math>, the verifier computes <math>A_0 = H(Y_i)</math> by hashing the public key of the one-time signature. For <math>j = 1, \ldots, n - 1</math>, the nodes of <math>A_j</math> of the path are computed with <math>A_j = H(A_{j-1} || \text{auth}_{j-1})</math>. If <math>A_n</math> equals the public key <math>\text{pub}</math> of the Merkle signature scheme, the signature is valid.
